about: How every SCE engine reads a <send> delay, written out by hand.
W3C SCXML 6.2 names the grammar: 'delay' and the value of 'delayexpr'
must be a valid CSS2 time. So one grammar, stated once, in ARCHITECTURE.md,
'Durations (Single Source of Truth)': surrounding whitespace aside, a
non-negative number - digits with an optional fraction of at least one
digit, or a leading '.' and digits; no sign, no exponent - followed
directly by the unit 'ms' or 's', either case. Anything else is not a
time: a static 'delay' is refused at build time, and a 'delayexpr' value
is the argument error of W3C SCXML 6.2 at run time.
The milliseconds are computed in exact decimal and truncated, never
through a float, so '1.005s' is 1005 on every engine rather than
whatever each float library rounds it to.
Why a shared table: measured 2026-09-28, nine parsers across seven
channels disagreed on eleven of fifteen inputs - a bare '5' was 5000 ms
on three of them and 5 ms on four, '1min' was a minute on two and nothing
elsewhere, '-1s' went negative on three - and no parser but the C++ one
had a test. A table read by all of them is the only thing that holds
them together.
Each case gives 'text' and 'ms': the milliseconds, or null when the text
is not a time.

cases.name: a fraction of a millisecond truncates
below a millisecond truncates to zero
a bare number has no unit
a bare fraction has no unit
minutes are not a CSS2 time unit
hours are not a CSS2 time unit
too large for a millisecond count
